appends.q: Give the correct order of stages in the wage relation as Marx analyses it, from the market exchange to the extraction of surplus value.
appends.a: The analysis runs: (1) Buyer and seller of labour-power meet as formal equals in the market (2) The worker sells labour-power for a wage equal to its reproduction cost (3) In production the capitalist consumes labour-power, which creates more value than the wage (4) The unpaid surplus value is appropriated as profit, so the fair-looking contract hides structural exploitation. A wrong answer that stops at the fair market exchange shows the student has confused the realm of circulation with the realm of production.

appends.q: Why does a Marxist hold that progressive taxation and welfare cannot by themselves achieve justice under capitalism?
appends.a: Redistribution only alters how surplus value is shared out after it has already been extracted in production; the wage relation stays intact, the capitalist class still controls the labour process and investment, and the worker remains a seller of labour-power. A wrong answer that calls welfare the fulfilment of justice shows the student has missed the Marxist distinction between distributing the surplus fairly and abolishing the class relation that produces it.

appends.q: What does the Veil of Ignorance exclude, and why does Marx treat that exclusion as a fatal flaw?
appends.a: Rawls' Veil of Ignorance excludes knowledge of one's class, social position, talents and conception of the good, modelling justice as a fair contract among abstract individuals; Marx objects that the basic structure of property and class is taken as given, so the procedure can never question the historical dispossession that created the starting positions. A wrong answer that praises the Veil for ignoring class shows the student has missed that ignoring class is precisely what Marx's historical materialism refuses to do.
